---
title: "Scope: what a scaling ladder predicts"
---

> **Reading note.** This is an explanatory reconstruction of Jiaxuan Zou’s literature synthesis. Published experiments belong to the cited teams. Numbered protocols and illustrative matrices are our planning synthesis unless explicitly attributed.

A scaling ladder is a designed collection of training runs. Each run varies a known quantity, while the remaining recipe is fixed or changes according to a declared rule. The blog's §1 distinguishes dense, mixture-of-experts (MoE), and data-constrained settings. This matters because a formula fitted to one setting need not apply to another.

## Questions and outputs

The central objects are model size $N$, training tokens $D$, compute $C$, and held-out loss $L$. A ladder can predict loss, select $N$ versus $D$ under a compute budget, compare recipes, or transfer hyperparameters. These are different estimation problems. A prescribed recipe can be evaluated without independently finding the best hyperparameters at every point; claiming the optimal frontier requires the latter effort.

For a dense model, distinguish trunk parameters $N_{\mathrm{body}}$ from embedding and head parameters. For MoE, record total and per-token active counts. For finite data, distinguish loss-bearing tokens $D$ from unique tokens $U$. These definitions determine what a fitted exponent means.

## Procedure

1. Write one target decision: for example, select model size under a fixed training budget.
2. Specify dense or MoE, intended token-to-parameter ratio, available unique data, context length, and deployment constraints.
3. Name the predicted quantity and its units. Cross-entropy in nats/token is different from bits/byte and benchmark accuracy.
4. Specify an extrapolation target and the largest fitting point. Reserve runs beyond that point for validation.

A useful starting relation is $C\approx6ND$, where $C$ is training FLOPs and $N$ is a compatible dense parameter count. It is an approximation; the measurement guide explains the omitted attention and head costs.

## Failure to watch

A smooth curve through small models establishes a fit, not a reliable large-model forecast. Delphi's failed initial recipe is the blog's motivating example; its stability failure is evidence for testing beyond the fitting regime, not evidence for a universal maximum extrapolation factor.

**Deliverable:** a one-page scope statement with the target, model/data regime, measurement definitions, and intended decision.

**Sources:** [blog §1](../reading/scientific-scaling-ladder.md#1-scope-and-terminology); [Marin, Delphi report](https://openathena.ai/blog/delphi/).
